meta.description: Gold karat purity table. Percentages are arithmetic (karat / 24). Legal/marketing context sourced to official regulation fetched 2026-10-22.
meta.no_hallucination_policy: Purity % = karat/24 (arithmetic, shown to 1dp). Fineness stamps shown are the standard millesimal equivalents used by assay authorities. Legal statements cite 16 CFR Part 23 (fetched 2026-10-22) and 15 U.S.C. ch.8 (fetched 2026-10-22).

karats.note: Fine gold (.999). Investment bullion standard; too soft for most ring wear.
Common in South Asian and Middle Eastern jewellery; offered as a hallmark fineness by the London Assay Office.
Luxury-tier standard in Europe; used by Cartier ('yellow gold 750/1000') and Tiffany ('18k').
The dominant US engagement-ring karat (Blue Nile, Brilliant Earth, Mejuri listings).
Historic US minimum to be called 'gold' before the FTC's 2018 revision.
Common UK/EU grade. The current FTC Guides' own example list includes '9 Karat Gold' as an acceptable karat designation when correctly disclosed (16 CFR 23.3(c)(1)).

legal_context.claim: A karat-quality marking must be correct: it is unfair or deceptive to misrepresent the quantity or karat fineness of gold in a product.
legal_context.evidence_quote: § 23.3(a): 'It is unfair or deceptive to misrepresent the presence of gold or gold alloy in an industry product, or the quantity or karat fineness of gold or gold alloy contained in the product...'

legal_context.claim: The word 'Gold' must be immediately preceded by a correct karat designation of at least equal conspicuousness (e.g. '14 Kt. Gold'), or be described by the karat designation alone (e.g. '14Kt.').
legal_context.evidence_quote: § 23.3(c)(1): '...immediately preceded by a correct designation of the karat fineness of the alloy, and such karat designation is of equal conspicuousness as the word "Gold" (for example, "14 Karat Gold", "14 K. Gold", "14 Kt. Gold", "9 Karat Gold", or "9 Kt. Gold").'

legal_context.claim: Hollow gold products must NOT be described as 'solid' gold.
legal_context.evidence_quote: § 23.3(c)(1): '...Such products should not be marked or described as "solid" or as being solidly of gold or of a gold alloy.'

legal_context.claim: A quality mark (e.g. '14K') must be accompanied by the trademark or name of the manufacturer/dealer (US National Stamping Act).
legal_context.evidence_quote: § 23.10: 'The National Stamping Act provides that any person... who applies or causes to be applied a quality mark... shall apply to the article the trademark or name of such person. [15 U.S.C. 297]'

legal_context.claim: US fineness tolerance: assayed as one piece including solder, the actual fineness may not be below the mark by more than 3/1000 (watchcases, flatware) or 7/1000 (other articles — rings included).
legal_context.evidence_quote: §295: '...shall not be less by more than three one-thousandth parts, in the case of a watchcase or flatware, or than seven one-thousandth parts, in the case of any other such article, than the fineness indicated by the mark...'

legal_context.claim: Falsely marked gold ware cannot lawfully be imported/exported or shipped in US interstate commerce.
legal_context.evidence_quote: §294: 'It shall be unlawful... to import or export or cause to be imported into or exported from the United States... any article of merchandise... made in whole or in part of gold or silver... and... indicating... that the gold or silver or alloy... is of a greater degree of fineness than the actual fineness...'

legal_context.claim: Gold-plated / gold-filled / rolled gold plate / gold overlay / electroplate are SURFACE coatings, not solid gold; each term has specific FTC fineness and durability conditions and requires the karat designation of the plating.
legal_context.evidence_quote: § 23.3(b)(5)-(8) and (c)(2): mechanical plating terms require 'a plating of gold alloy of not less than 10 karat fineness and of reasonable durability... when such plating constitutes at least 1/40th of the weight of the metal in the entire article...'

legal_context.claim: UK hallmarking is performed by independent assay offices (e.g. the Goldsmiths' Company Assay Office, hallmarking since 1300); standard gold finenesses include 9, 14, 18, 22 ct, 990 and 999.
legal_context.evidence_quote: '...hallmarking began... since 1300 when we first began testing and hallmarking precious metals.' Calculator metal list: 'Gold (14 Carat), Gold (18 carat), Gold (22 carat), Gold (9 carat), Gold (990), Gold (999)'.

legal_context.claim: Diamond/metal weight claims are regulated: it is unfair or deceptive to misrepresent weight; a carat = 200 mg exactly.
legal_context.evidence_quote: § 23.18(a),(b): 'It is unfair or deceptive to misrepresent the weight of a diamond.' 'A carat is a standard unit of weight for a diamond and is equivalent to 200 milligrams (1/5 gram).'

warning: SECONDARY-SOURCE DISCREPANCY (found during hallucination audit): several retail blogs claim US law allows a '0.5 karat' tolerance below the stamp (e.g. 'a 14K stamp can assay 13.5K'). The official statute (15 U.S.C. §295, as amended 1976) instead sets whole-article tolerances of 7/1000 fineness (~0.17 karat at 14K) for rings. Do not rely on the 0.5-karat figure — see Flagged item F9.
A stamp alone is not proof. The FTC Guides regulate CLAIMS; independent verification of an individual piece requires assay (e.g. XRF) by an independent jeweler/assay office.
